彎管號主要用於文藝復興時期，十六世紀已在西班牙使用，普魯士宮廷樂隊抄本、1617: The crumhorn belongs mainly to the Renaissance; it was already in use in Spain in the sixteenth century, and traces of it appear in a manuscript set of parts from the Prussian court band, in a work of 1617 and in a letter of 1526, and it was also suggested as a substitute for the trombone and others in sacred vocal music. Since the 1960s the early-music revival has brought it back into playing.
彎管號以風帽內的雙簧片發聲，吹氣通過風帽開口使簧片振動，音高由按孔開閉改變。其音: The crumhorn sounds from a double reed inside a wind cap: the player blows through an opening in the cap and the reed vibrates, and the pitch changes as the fingerholes are opened and closed. Its timbre has a marked buzzing quality, quieter than the rauschpfeife and the shawm of the same family, which have conical bores. The range is usually a ninth, and in practice playing stays within the fundamental series, since the reed is not in the mouth and overblowing is difficult. Larger instruments can extend downwards with added holes, keys and a slide, and the pitch can be lowered a fourth by reducing the wind pressure; modern instruments with keys reach up to an eleventh. Cross-fingering gives the semitones, except for the minor second above the lowest note.
彎管號是文藝復興時期歐洲德語地區常見的雙簧木管樂器，Hornbostel–Sac: The crumhorn is a double-reed woodwind common in the German-speaking lands of Europe in the Renaissance, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.111.2. Its construction resembles a bagpipe chanter: the double reed sits inside a long wind cap, the player blows through a slit in the cap to sound it, and the pitch is changed with fingerholes; the end of the pipe curves up into a J shape, which is purely decorative. Because the range is limited, instruments of different sizes are often formed into a consort imitating a vocal quartet, and it also appears in the Prussian court band and in sacred vocal works. 19

彎管號的發聲體為雙簧片，裝於長形風帽內，管身開有指孔，末端向上彎曲。來源資料僅說: The sounding body of the crumhorn is a double reed set inside a long wind cap, with fingerholes in the pipe and the end curving upward. The source describes only this kind of construction and does not record the particular materials of the reed, the cap, the pipe or any other part, nor does it mention any material that could be inferred.
彎管號的雙簧片裝在長風帽內，吹奏者不將簧片入口，而是由風帽上的槽吹氣發聲。初學先: The crumhorn's double reed sits inside a long wind cap, and the player does not take the reed into the mouth but blows through a slit in the cap. A beginner first opens and closes the fingerholes on the pipe, practising the blowing and the basic order of holes; because the reed is not in the mouth, overblowing is difficult, and usually only the fundamental series is used. Semitones, when needed, come from cross-fingering, except for the minor second above the lowest note.
彎管號見於文藝復興時期歐洲德語地區的早期音樂場合，也因二十世紀六十年代古樂復興而: The crumhorn appears in early-music settings in the German-speaking lands of Renaissance Europe, and reappeared with the revival of early music in the 1960s. It is often formed into a consort of instruments at different pitches, imitating the four voices of soprano, alto, tenor and bass; the sources show a manuscript set of parts from the Prussian court band, the paduana for four crumhorns in Schein's Banchetto Musicale, Stoltzer's Erzürne dich nicht, and Praetorius's use of it in place of the trombone and bassoon in sacred vocal works.
